sentences.t: Sigon þā tō slǣpe.
sentences.l: They sank then to sleep.
sentences.i: Then they sank into sleep.
sentences.n: ‘Sigon’ is the third person plural past of ‘sīgan’, ‘sink, sag’, so ‘they sank’; the subject is the Danes and Geats who have bedded down in Heorot at the end of the last part. ‘tō slǣpe’ is ‘to sleep’, ‘slǣpe’ being the dative.

sentences.t:
Sum sāre angeald
ǣfenræste, swā him ful oft gelamp,
siþðan goldsele Grendel warode,
unriht æfnde, oþ þæt ende becwōm,
swylt æfter synnum.
sentences.l: One sorely paid for evening-rest, as to them very often happened, since Grendel warded the gold-hall, practiced wrong, until the end came, death after sins.
sentences.i: One of them paid dearly for that night’s rest, as had very often happened to them ever since Grendel took over the gold hall and went on with his wrongdoing, until the end came to him, death for his sins.
sentences.n: ‘Sum’ is ‘one’, nominative singular, ‘one of them’; who the one is is not said here. ‘angeald’ is the past of ‘ongieldan’, ‘pay for, suffer for’, and ‘ǣfenræste’ (‘ǣfen’ evening + ‘ræst’ rest) is what he paid for; the form does not show its case. ‘swā him ful oft gelamp’ is ‘as to them very often befell’, ‘him’ being plural. ‘goldsele’ is ‘gold-hall’ (Heorot); ‘warode’ is the past of ‘warian’, ‘guard, hold, inhabit’, a verb close in sense to ‘weardode’ at fitt 1 line 104, which the published part renders ‘warded’ (‘warian’ and ‘weardian’ are different verbs, but both mean ‘guard, hold’). In the second half the subject is still Grendel: ‘unriht æfnde’, ‘practiced wrong’ (‘æfnan’ is ‘perform, carry out’). In ‘oþ þæt ende becwōm’, ‘ende’ is the subject of ‘becwōm’ (‘came’), and ‘swylt’ (death) stands beside it; it is Grendel’s end, ‘after’, that is, because of, his sins (‘æfter synnum’, dative plural).

sentences.t:
Þæt gesȳne wearþ,
wīdcūþ werum, þætte wrecend þā gȳt
lifde æfter lāþum, lange þrāge,
æfter gūðceare;
sentences.l: That became visible, widely known to men, that an avenger still then lived after the hated one, a long time, after war-care;
sentences.i: It became plain, and widely known among men, that an avenger was still alive after the hateful one, and lived on a long while after the grief of the fight;
sentences.n: ‘Þæt gesȳne wearþ, wīdcūþ werum’ is ‘that became plain, widely known to men’; ‘gesȳne’ is an adjective, ‘visible, evident’, and ‘werum’ a dative plural, ‘to men’. ‘þætte’ is ‘þæt þe’, simply ‘that’, and opens the clause that says what became known: ‘wrecend’ (an avenger, nominative) ‘þā gȳt lifde’, ‘was still living’. ‘æfter lāþum’ is ‘after the hated one’, that is Grendel; the dative ‘lāþum’ could also be plural, ‘the hated ones’, and I take the singular. ‘lange þrāge’ is an accusative of time, ‘a long while’. ‘gūðceare’ is ‘gūð’ war + ‘cearu’ sorrow, ‘war-grief’; Trautmann prints ‘gūðsceare’ (apparatus), which would be ‘war-destruction’. Which fight is meant, and whose sorrow, is left open. Klaeber ends the unit with a semicolon, and the name of the avenger follows.

sentences.t:
Grendles mōdor,
ides āglǣcwīf yrmþe gemunde,
sē þe wæteregesan wunian scolde,
cealde strēamas, siþðan Cāin wearð
tō ecgbanan āngan brēþer,
fæderenmǣge;
sentences.l: Grendel’s mother, lady, awesome-woman, remembered misery, he who the water-terrors to dwell had to, the cold streams, since Cain became to an edge-slayer for his only brother, father-kinsman;
sentences.i: It was Grendel’s mother, a lady and a fearsome woman, who remembered her misery, she who had to live in the terrible waters, the cold streams, ever since Cain became the slayer by the sword of his only brother, his kinsman on the father’s side;
sentences.n: ‘Grendles mōdor’ is the subject; ‘ides’ (‘lady, woman’) and ‘āglǣcwīf’ (‘āglǣca’, the awesome one, as the published parts render it, + ‘wīf’ woman) are in apposition. ‘yrmþe gemunde’: ‘gemunan’ takes the genitive, so ‘remembered her misery’. ‘sē þe’ is masculine though the woman is meant; some editors print ‘sē[o]’ (apparatus) to make it feminine. ‘wæteregesan’ occurs only here: ‘wæter’ + ‘egesa’ (terror), and ‘terrible waters’ is a guess at its force; the following ‘cealde strēamas’ is in apposition. ‘wunian scolde’ is ‘had to dwell’. Then the poem goes back to Cain, the ‘kin of Cain’ of line 104: ‘tō ecgbanan’ is ‘as an edge-slayer’ (‘ecg’ edge, ‘bana’ slayer), ‘āngan brēþer’ a dative, ‘his only brother’, and ‘fæderenmǣge’ (‘fæderen’ of the father’s side + ‘mǣg’ kinsman) a dative in apposition; it is rare, and ‘kinsman by the father’ is the reading from the lexica. Klaeber’s ‘Cāin’ has an italic ‘in’ because the manuscript reads ‘camp’, and Grundtvig and Kemble set ‘Cāin’ right.

sentences.t:
hē þā fāg gewāt,
morþre gemearcod mandrēam fleôn,
wēsten warode.
sentences.l: he then guilty departed, marked by murder, to flee the joy of men; the wasteland he warded.
sentences.i: Then, an outlaw marked by his murder, he went away to flee the company of men, and he kept to the wilderness.
sentences.n: ‘fāg’ is the adjective the glossary gives as ‘hostile, at feud, guilty’; here Cain is ‘guilty’ or ‘outlawed’. ‘morþre gemearcod’ is ‘marked by murder’ (‘morþre’ dative, the means; ‘gemearcod’ a past participle). ‘mandrēam fleôn’ is ‘to flee human joy’: ‘mandrēam’ (‘mann’ man + ‘drēam’ joy) is the object, and the infinitive ‘fleôn’ gives the purpose (Klaeber prints a circumflex over the ‘eô’, as at ‘seôn’, 1275). ‘wēsten warode’ is ‘warded (kept) the wasteland’, with ‘warode’ as at 1253, and ‘wēsten’ an accusative.

sentences.t:
Þanon wōc fela
geōsceaftgāsta;
sentences.l: Thence awoke many fate-ghosts;
sentences.i: From him there sprang many spirits of doom;
sentences.n: ‘Þanon’ is ‘from there, from him’, that is from Cain. ‘wōc’ is the past of ‘wæcnan’, ‘awake, spring up, be born’, and ‘fela’ takes the genitive plural: ‘many of …’. ‘geōsceaftgāsta’ is a compound of ‘gāst’ (spirit) with ‘geōsceaft’, a word that means ‘what is decreed’, whether fate or creation; Kluge and Holthausen (apparatus) read the first part as an old stressed form of the prefix in ‘gesceaft’ (‘geasceaft’). ‘Fate-ghosts’ is therefore a guess, and ‘spirits of doom’ in the idiomatic version is a guess too.

sentences.l: was of those Grendel one, a sword-felon, hateful, who at Heorot found a waking man to await battle;
sentences.i: Grendel was one of them, a savage outcast, hostile, who at Heorot found a man awake and waiting for battle;
sentences.n: ‘wæs þǣra Grendel sum’ is ‘Grendel was one of those’, ‘þǣra’ being the genitive plural and ‘sum’ ‘one’. ‘heorowearh’ occurs nowhere else: ‘wearh’ is ‘outlaw, felon, accursed being’, and ‘heoru’ is ‘sword, blade’, but as a first element it may simply mean ‘fierce’, so ‘sword-felon’ in the literal version and ‘savage outcast’ in the idiomatic are guesses. ‘hetelīc’ is ‘hateful, hostile’. ‘sē … fand’ is ‘who found’, and the accusative ‘wæccendne wer’ is ‘a watching man’, that is Beowulf, with ‘wīges bīdan’, ‘to await (genitive) battle’.

sentences.t: þǣr him āglǣca ætgrǣpe wearð;
sentences.l: there to him the awesome one became gripping;
sentences.i: there the fearsome one laid hold of him;
sentences.n: ‘þǣr’ is ‘there’, ‘him’ the dative, ‘to him’. ‘wearð’ is the past of ‘weorþan’, ‘become’. ‘ætgrǣpe’ is a rare word taken as an adjective, ‘gripping, laying hold’; the sense ‘laid hold of him’ is a guess from the lexica. ‘āglǣca’ is the awesome one, Grendel, as in the earlier parts.

sentences.t:
hwæþre hē gemunde mægenes strenge,
gimfæste gife, ðē him God sealde,
ond him tō Anwaldan āre gelȳfde,
frōfre ond fultum;
sentences.l: However he remembered the strength of his might, the ample gift that God gave him, and for himself in the Sole-ruler for favor trusted, comfort and help;
sentences.i: Yet he remembered the strength of his might, the splendid gift that God had given him, and trusted in the Sole Ruler for favor, comfort and help;
sentences.n: ‘hwæþre’ is ‘however, yet’. ‘gemunde’ takes the genitive, so ‘mægenes strenge’ is ‘the strength of his might’ (‘strenge’ is a form of ‘strengu’ that serves for genitive, dative or accusative; here it is the object), with ‘gimfæste gife’ in apposition, ‘the gift that God gave him’ (‘ðē’ is ‘þe’, ‘which’). ‘gimfæste’ is rare, ‘gim’ gem + ‘fæst’ firm, and ‘ample’ or ‘splendid’ is a guess. ‘Anwaldan’ (‘ān’ one + ‘wealda’ ruler) is God, ‘the Sole Ruler’, a title like the house ‘Fæder alwalda’ (‘Father all-ruler’, fitt 4). ‘him tō Anwaldan āre gelȳfde’ is ‘trusted for himself in the Sole Ruler for favor’, ‘him’ being a dative of interest, and ‘frōfre ond fultum’ (comfort and help) add to ‘āre’. Beowulf’s trust in God is told here as the reason he was not overcome.

sentences.t:
ðȳ hē þone fēond ofercwōm,
gehnǣgde helle gāst.
sentences.l: Therefore he overcame the foe, brought low the hell-spirit.
sentences.i: So he overcame the fiend and brought low the spirit of hell.
sentences.n: ‘ðȳ’ is the instrumental of ‘se’, ‘by that’, ‘therefore’, and ‘ofercwōm’ the past of ‘ofercuman’, ‘overcome’. ‘gehnǣgde’ is the past of ‘gehnǣgan’, ‘bring low, humble’, and ‘helle gāst’ is ‘spirit of hell’, in apposition to ‘fēond’; the poet puts the earlier fight in a line and a half and goes on.

sentences.t:
Þā hē hēan gewāt,
drēame bedǣled dēaþwīc seôn,
mancynnes fēond.
sentences.l: Then he abject departed, of joy deprived, the death-dwelling to see, the foe of mankind.
sentences.i: Then the enemy of mankind went away, humbled and robbed of joy, to see his dwelling of death.
sentences.n: ‘hēan’ is the adjective meaning ‘abject, humiliated’ (a different word from ‘hēah’, ‘high’); ‘gewāt’ is ‘departed’. ‘drēame bedǣled’ is ‘deprived of joy’ (‘bedǣlan’ takes the dative, and the participle ‘bedǣled’ comes after it). ‘dēaþwīc seôn’ is ‘to see the death-dwelling’ (‘wīc’ dwelling): the infinitive gives the purpose, and the place is his lair, where he is to die. ‘mancynnes fēond’ is ‘foe of mankind’, as at line 164.

sentences.t:
Ond his mōdor þā gȳt
gīfre ond galgmōd gegān wolde
sorhfulne sīð, sunu dēoð wrecan.
sentences.l: And his mother yet greedy and gallows-minded wished to go a sorrowful journey, the son’s death to avenge.
sentences.i: And his mother, still greedy and grim-hearted, meant to go on a grievous journey to avenge her son’s death.
sentences.n: ‘Ond his mōdor þā gȳt’ is ‘and his mother yet’. ‘gīfre’ is ‘greedy, eager’. ‘galgmōd’ has ‘galga’, gallows, and ‘mōd’, mind; ‘gallows-minded’ is a literal reading, and ‘grim-hearted’ a guess at what it implies (the Bosworth–Toller entry gives ‘gloomy’). ‘gegān wolde sorhfulne sīð’ is ‘wished to go a sorrowful journey’ (‘sīð’ accusative). Klaeber’s last words are changed: the manuscript has ‘sunu þeod’, and ‘dēoð’, with the italic ‘d’, is his reading of ‘þeod’ as an error for ‘dēað’ (‘death’), and ‘sunu’ is taken as a genitive, ‘of the son’. Earlier editors read ‘suna dēað’ (apparatus). ‘wrecan’ is ‘avenge’, the verb of ‘wrecend’ in 1256.

sentences.t:
Cōm þā tō Heorote, ðǣr Hring-Dene
geond þæt sæld swǣfun.
sentences.l: She came then to Heorot, where the Ring-Danes throughout the hall slept.
sentences.i: She came to Heorot, where the Ring-Danes lay asleep throughout the hall.
sentences.n: The subject of ‘Cōm’ is the mother of the last unit. ‘Hring-Dene’ is nominative plural, the ‘Ring-Danes’ of line 116, and ‘swǣfun’ the past plural of ‘swefan’, ‘sleep’. ‘geond þæt sæld’ is ‘throughout that hall’ (‘sæld’ is a neuter, ‘dwelling, hall’, related to ‘sele’).

sentences.t:
Þā ðǣr sōna wearð
edhwyrft eorlum, siþðan inne fealh
Grendles mōdor.
sentences.l: Then there soon was a reversal to the earls, after in pressed Grendel’s mother.
sentences.i: Then at once things were turned about for the earls, as soon as Grendel’s mother had forced her way in.
sentences.n: ‘edhwyrft’ is ‘ed-’ back + ‘hwyrft’ turn, a ‘turning back’, here a reversal of fortune, the sense taken from the lexica; ‘eorlum’ is a dative, ‘for the earls’. ‘siþðan’ is ‘after, when’. ‘inne fealh’ is the past of ‘feolan’, ‘press on, force one’s way’, with ‘inne’ ‘within’ (in line 1200 the manuscript has the same form ‘fealh’, which editors change there to ‘flēah’; here it stands).

sentences.t:
Wæs se gryre lǣssa
efne swā micle, swā bið mægþa cræft,
wīggryre wīfes be wǣpnedmen,
þonne heoru bunden, hamere geþrūen,
sweord swāte fāh swīn ofer helme
ecgum dyhtig andweard scireð.
sentences.l: The terror was less just so much as is the might of maidens, woman’s war-terror, by a weaponed man, when a blade bound, by hammer forged, a sword blood-stained, the boar over the helmet, strong with edges, facing shears.
sentences.i: The terror was less by just as much as a woman’s strength, a woman’s war-terror, is less than an armed man’s, when the bound blade, hammer-forged, the sword stained with blood, doughty in its edges, cuts through the boar-crest on the helmet it faces.
sentences.n: The comparison is built on ‘lǣssa efne swā micle, swā …’: ‘less by just as much as …’. ‘mægþa cræft’ (‘mægþ’ girl, maiden, genitive plural; ‘cræft’ strength) and ‘wīggryre wīfes’ (‘war-terror of a woman’) are two names for the same thing; ‘be wǣpnedmen’ is ‘beside an armed man’, with ‘wǣpnedmen’ a dative singular (the mutated form of ‘mann’), ‘a man’ in the sense of a male. The picture is of the sword in the second half. ‘heoru bunden’ is ‘the bound blade’, which probably means a hilt or blade bound with metal; ‘geþrūen’ is the correction of Sievers (and, with a query, Grein) of the manuscript’s ‘geþuren’, and I take it from a rare verb meaning ‘press, force’, so ‘hammer-forged’ is a guess. ‘swāte fāh’ is ‘stained with blood’ (‘fāh’ in its sense ‘coloured’). ‘swīn ofer helme’ is the boar-image on the helmet, the object of ‘scireð’, which I take as ‘cuts’ (‘scieran’, to shear, cut). ‘ecgum dyhtig’ is ‘strong in its edges’. ‘andweard’ means ‘facing, present’: whether it goes with the sword or with the boar is not settled, and I read it with the sword.

sentences.l: Then was in the hall the hard-edged sword drawn over the seats, many a broad shield lifted fast in hand;
sentences.i: Then in the hall the hard-edged sword was drawn above the benches, and many a broad shield was raised, held fast in the hand;
sentences.n: ‘heardecg’ is an adjective, ‘hard-edged’, going with ‘sweord’, and ‘togen’ the past participle of ‘tēon’, ‘drawn’; ‘ofer setlum’ is ‘over the seats’. ‘sīdrand’ is ‘wide shield’ (‘sīd’ broad + ‘rand’ shield-rim), the subject of the second passive: ‘manig sīdrand hafen’, ‘many a shield raised’ (‘hafen’ is the participle of ‘hebban’). ‘handa fæst’ is ‘fast in the hand’; ‘handa’ is a dative and serves as ‘in hand’.

sentences.t:
helm ne gemunde,
byrnan sīde, þā hine se brōga angeat.
sentences.l: A helmet he did not remember, a broad byrnie, when him the terror seized.
sentences.i: When the terror took hold of him, each man gave no thought to helmet or broad mail-coat.
sentences.n: ‘gemunde’ is singular and ‘ne gemunde’ is ‘did not think of’; the subject is each man as he is caught, so the singular ‘hine’ (‘him’) means any one of them. ‘gemunan’ ordinarily takes the genitive, but ‘helm’ shows no case, and ‘byrnan sīde’ (‘wide byrnie’) is another form that could be accusative. ‘se brōga’ is ‘the terror’, and ‘angeat’ the past of ‘ongietan’, ‘perceive, grasp’; ‘seized’ is a loose rendering. Grein would read ‘þe’ for ‘þā’ (apparatus), which makes ‘the terror that seized him’ a relative clause.

sentences.t:
Hēo wæs on ofste, wolde ūt þanon,
fēore beorgan, þā hēo onfunden wæs;
sentences.l: She was in haste, wished out from there, to save her life, when she was discovered;
sentences.i: She was in a hurry and wanted to be out of there, to save her life, now that she was discovered;
sentences.n: ‘on ofste’ is ‘in haste’. ‘wolde ūt þanon’ lacks a verb of motion, which ‘wolde’ makes understood: ‘wished (to go) out from there’. ‘fēore beorgan’ is ‘to save her life’ (‘feorh’, life, in the dative with ‘beorgan’, ‘protect, spare’). ‘onfunden wæs’ is the passive of ‘onfindan’, ‘find out, detect’.

sentences.t:
hraðe hēo æþelinga ānne hæfde
fæste befangen, þā hēo tō fenne gang.
sentences.l: Quickly she one of the princes had fast seized, when she to the fen went.
sentences.i: In a moment she had seized one of the princes and held him fast, as she made for the fen.
sentences.n: ‘hæfde … befangen’ is a perfect, ‘had seized’ (‘befōn’, to grasp, encompass), with ‘ānne’ (‘one’, accusative) as its object and ‘æþelinga’ the genitive plural, ‘of the princes’. ‘fæste’ is ‘firmly’. ‘gang’ is the past of ‘gangan’, ‘went’, and ‘fenne’ the dative of ‘fen’, ‘fen, marsh’, with ‘tō’.

sentences.t:
Sē wæs Hrōþgāre hæleþa lēofost
on gesīðes hād be sǣm twēonum,
rīce randwiga, þone ðe hēo on ræste ābrēat,
blǣdfæstne beorn.
sentences.l: He was to Hrothgar of heroes dearest in the rank of companion between the seas, a mighty shield-warrior, him whom she in his rest killed, a glory-firm man.
sentences.i: He was the dearest to Hrothgar of all heroes in the rank of companion anywhere between the seas, a strong shield-warrior, the one she killed as he lay at rest, a man firm in glory.
sentences.n: The unnamed victim is introduced by ‘Sē wæs Hrōþgāre hæleþa lēofost’, ‘he was to Hrothgar the dearest of heroes’ (‘Hrōþgāre’ dative, ‘hæleþa’ genitive plural, ‘lēofost’ superlative of ‘lēof’). ‘on gesīðes hād’ is ‘in the rank of companion’ (‘hād’ is rank, condition); ‘be sǣm twēonum’ is ‘between the two seas’, an expression for ‘anywhere in the world’. ‘rīce randwiga’ is ‘mighty shield-warrior’ (‘rand’ shield). ‘þone ðe hēo on ræste ābrēat’ is ‘whom she destroyed in his rest’ (‘ābrēotan’ is ‘destroy, kill’), and ‘blǣdfæstne’ is ‘firm in glory’ (‘blǣd’ glory or success + ‘fæst’), an accusative in apposition to ‘þone’.

sentences.t:
Næs Bēowulf ðǣr,
ac wæs ōþer in ǣr geteohhod
æfter māþðumgife mǣrum Gēate.
sentences.l: Not-was Beowulf there, but was another lodging earlier assigned, after the treasure-giving, to the famous Geat.
sentences.i: Beowulf was not there; another lodging had been assigned to the famous Geat earlier, after the giving of treasure.
sentences.n: ‘Næs’ is ‘ne wæs’, ‘was not’. ‘ōþer in’ I take as ‘another lodging’, ‘in’ being a noun, ‘dwelling’; ‘geteohhod’ is the past participle of ‘geteohhian’, ‘appoint, assign’, and ‘ǣr’ is ‘earlier’. ‘æfter māþðumgife’ is ‘after the treasure-giving’ (‘māþðum’ treasure + ‘gifu’ gift), the gifts of fitt 18, and ‘mǣrum Gēate’ a dative, ‘to the famous Geat’, Beowulf.

sentences.t:
Hrēam wearð in Heorote; hēo under heolfre genam
cūþe folme;
sentences.l: Outcry was in Heorot; she under gore took the known hand;
sentences.i: A cry went up in Heorot; she took the hand she knew from under the gore;
sentences.n: ‘hrēam’ is a masculine noun, ‘outcry’. ‘heolfre’ is a dative, ‘gore, blood’, and ‘under heolfre’ is hard to place; I take it as ‘beneath the blood’, that is with blood about it, and the sense is uncertain. ‘cūþe folme’ is ‘the known hand’, accusative: probably the arm and hand of her son, torn off in Beowulf’s fight and left behind at line 970 and seen hanging under the roof at line 983, fitt 14. That the hand is Grendel’s is an inference from the earlier parts; this passage does not say so.

sentences.t:
cearu wæs genīwod,
geworden in wīcun.
sentences.l: Sorrow was renewed, become in the dwellings.
sentences.i: Their sorrow was made new, come upon the homes of the Danes.
sentences.n: ‘cearu’ is ‘sorrow’, the subject, and ‘genīwod’ the participle, ‘renewed’; ‘geworden’ is the participle of ‘weorþan’, ‘become, come about’. ‘wīcun’ is the dative plural of ‘wīc’, ‘dwelling’.

sentences.t:
Ne wæs þæt gewrixle til,
þæt hīe on bā healfa bicgan scoldon
frēonda fēorum!
sentences.l: Not was that exchange good, that they on both sides had to pay with friends’ lives!
sentences.i: That was no good bargain, that both sides had to pay for it with the lives of friends!
sentences.n: ‘gewrixle’ is a neuter, ‘exchange, trade’, and ‘til’ ‘good’. ‘hīe’ is ‘they’, ‘on bā healfa’ ‘on both sides’ (‘healfa’ is the accusative plural). ‘bicgan’ is ‘buy’, here ‘pay for’, and ‘frēonda fēorum’ is the dative plural of ‘feorh’ (life) with the genitive plural of ‘frēond’: the lives of friends are the price. The exclamation mark is Klaeber’s.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs frōd cyning,
hār hilderinc on hrēon mōde,
syðþan hē aldorþegn unlyfigendne,
þone dēorestan dēadne wisse.
sentences.l: Then was the old king, the hoary battle-warrior, in a troubled mind, after he the chief-thane lifeless, the dearest, dead knew.
sentences.i: Then the wise old king, the grey battle-warrior, was in a troubled mood, once he knew that his chief thane was lifeless, dead, the dearest of men.
sentences.n: ‘frōd’ is ‘wise, old’, ‘hār’ ‘grey-haired’, and ‘hilderinc’ ‘battle-warrior’, all in apposition to ‘cyning’. ‘on hrēon mōde’ is ‘in troubled mind’ (‘hrēoh’, stormy, troubled, in the dative). ‘syðþan’ is ‘since, after’. ‘wisse’ is the past of ‘witan’, ‘knew’, with ‘aldorþegn’ (‘chief thane’, ‘aldor’ lord or life) as the accusative object, and ‘unlyfigendne’ (‘not living’), ‘þone dēorestan’ (‘the dearest’) and ‘dēadne’ (‘dead’) agreeing with it.

sentences.t:
Hraþe wæs tō būre Bēowulf fetod,
sigorēadig secg.
sentences.l: Quickly was to the bower Beowulf fetched, victory-blessed man.
sentences.i: Beowulf was quickly fetched to the chamber, the man blessed with victory.
sentences.n: ‘fetod’ is the past participle of ‘fetian’, ‘fetch’, and ‘būre’ the dative of ‘būr’, ‘chamber’ (whose chamber is not said; the next unit has the king waiting, so the king’s bower is likely). ‘sigorēadig’ is ‘sigor’ victory + ‘ēadig’ blessed, with ‘secg’ ‘man’ in apposition.

sentences.t:
Samod ǣrdæge
ēode eorla sum, æþele cempa
self mid gesīðum þǣr se snotera bād,
hwæþer him Alwalda ǣfre wille
æfter wēaspelle wyrpe gefremman.
sentences.l: At the same time as early day went one of the earls, the noble champion himself with his companions, where the wise one waited, whether for him the All-ruler ever would after the woe-tale bring about a change.
sentences.i: At daybreak one of the earls, the noble champion, himself went with his companions to where the wise king waited to see whether the Ruler of all would ever bring about a change for him after the grievous news.
sentences.n: ‘samod ǣrdæge’ is ‘together with early day’, at first light (‘ǣrdæge’, dative). ‘ēode’ is the past of ‘gān’, ‘went’; ‘eorla sum’ is ‘one of the earls’, and ‘æþele cempa’ ‘noble champion’, both naming Beowulf, with ‘self’ (‘himself’). ‘þǣr se snotera bād’ is ‘where the wise one waited’ (‘bād’ past of ‘bīdan’), the king. The clause that follows says what he waited for: ‘hwæþer’ is ‘whether’, Sievers’ and later editors’ reading (the manuscript has ‘hwæþre’, ‘however’, so the italic ‘er’ marks his change), ‘Alwalda’ has an italic ‘l’ (the manuscript has ‘alf walda’; Thorpe set the ‘l’ right) and means ‘All-ruler’, God, as at line 955. ‘wille’ is the present subjunctive, with ‘him’ (‘for him’, the king) before it. ‘wēaspelle’ is ‘woe-tale’ (‘wēa’ woe + ‘spell’ tale), ‘wyrpe’ ‘turn, change for the better’, and ‘gefremman’ ‘bring about’.

sentences.t:
Gang ðā æfter flōre fyrdwyrðe man
mid his handscale — healwudu dynede —,
sentences.l: Went then along the floor the war-worthy man with his hand-troop — the hall-wood resounded —,
sentences.i: Then the man of battle-worth strode along the floor with his band of followers — the timbers of the hall rang —,
sentences.n: ‘Gang’ is the past of ‘gangan’, ‘went’, and ‘æfter flōre’ ‘along the floor’. ‘fyrdwyrðe man’ is ‘war-worthy man’ (‘fyrd’ army, host), a man of proven worth in the field, Beowulf. ‘handscale’ is hard: it seems to be ‘hand’ + ‘scalu’, a ‘band’ of followers, and ‘hand-troop’ is a guess; Thorpe and others read ‘-scole’ (apparatus), but the sense is the same. The dashes mark a parenthesis, ‘healwudu dynede’, ‘the hall-wood (the timbers) resounded’ (‘dynian’, ‘resound, din’).

sentences.t:
þæt hē þone wīsan wordum nǣgde
frēan Ingwina,
sentences.l: that he the wise one with words addressed, the lord of the Ingwine,
sentences.i: so that he could speak to the wise one, the lord of the Danes,
sentences.n: ‘þæt’ gives purpose, ‘so that’. ‘nǣgde’ is Grein’s correction: the manuscript has ‘hnægde’, and ‘nǣgan’ is ‘accost, address’; the italic ‘n’ marks the changed word-beginning, the ‘h’ being gone. Other editors read ‘nēgde’; ‘hnǣgan’, ‘bow down’, as at ‘gehnǣgde’ (1274), would be another word. ‘þone wīsan’ is ‘the wise one’, Hrothgar, and ‘wordum’ ‘with words’. ‘frēan Ingwina’ is ‘lord of the Ingwine’, a poetic name for the Danes, in apposition; the glossary has ‘friends of Ing’.

sentences.t:
frægn gif him wǣre
æfter nēodlaðu[m] niht getǣse.
sentences.l: asked if for him it was, after urgent invitations, a night comfortable.
sentences.i: and asked whether the night had been an easy one for him, after such pressing invitations.
sentences.n: ‘frægn’ is the past of ‘fregnan’, ‘ask’; ‘gif’ ‘if, whether’; ‘him’ ‘for him’; ‘wǣre’ the past subjunctive of the question, ‘had been’. ‘niht getǣse’ is ‘a comfortable night’ (‘getǣse’, ‘agreeable, convenient’, a rare adjective). ‘nēodlaðu[m]’ is mended: the manuscript has ‘neod laðu’, and Klaeber adds the ending ‘-m’ to make the dative plural; ‘nēod’ is ‘desire, urgency’ and ‘laðu’ ‘invitation’, so ‘after urgent invitations’ is a guess, and who invited whom is not said. Sweet read ‘-laðe’ and Cosijn ‘nēadlāðum’, ‘compulsory invitations’ (apparatus).
